etymologies.etymologyHTML: Originally a verb of uncertain etymology. Possibly from French esclachier (“to break”). Used in the Wycliffe Bible as slascht (see 1 Kings 5:18) but otherwise unattested until 16th century. Conjunctive use from various applications of the punctuation mark ⟨/⟩. See also slash fiction.

definitions.definition: A swift, broad cutting stroke, especially one made with an edged weapon or whip.
(sports) A wide striking motion made with an implement such as a cricket bat, hockey stick, or lacrosse stick.
(figuratively) A sharp reduction in resources allotted.
A slashing action or motion:
A deep cut or laceration, as made by an edged weapon or whip.
(botany) A deep taper-pointed incision in a plant.
A mark made by slashing:
(fashion) A slit in an outer garment, usually exposing a lining or inner garment of a contrasting color or design.
(US and Canada) A clearing in a forest, particularly one made by logging, fire, or other violent action.

quote.citation: 1895, Henry Van Dyke, Little Rivers: A Book of Essays in Profitable Idleness:
quote.text: We passed over the shoulder of a ridge and around the edge of a fire slash, and then we had the mountain fairly before us.

definitions.definition: (often proscribed) Any similar typographical mark, such as the backslash ⟨\⟩.
(originally US, typography) The slash mark: the punctuation mark ⟨/⟩.

quote.citation: 1965, Dmitri A. Borgmann, Language on Vacation, page 240:
quote.text: Initial inquiries among professional typists uncover names like slant, slant line, slash, and slash mark. Examination of typing instruction manuals discloses additional names such as diagonal and diagonal mark, and other sources provide the designation oblique.

definitions.definition: (vulgar, slang) The vulva.
Something resembling such a mark:
(US and Canada) The loose woody debris remaining from a slash; the trimmings left while preparing felled trees for removal.
(fandom slang) Slash fiction; fan fiction focused on homoerotic pairing of fictional characters.

quote.citation: 2013, Katherine Arcement, “Diary”, in London Review of Books, volume 35, number 5:
quote.text: Comments merely allow readers to proclaim themselves mortally offended by the content of a story, despite having been warned in large block letters of INCEST or SLASH (any kind of sex between two men or two women: the term originated with the Kirk/Spock pairing – it described the literal slash between their names).

definitions.definition: To cut with a swift broad stroke of an edged weapon.
To produce a similar wound with a savage strike of a whip.
(ice hockey) To strike swiftly and laterally with a hockey stick, usually across another player's arms or legs.
(figuratively) To reduce sharply.
(fashion) To create slashes in a garment.
(figuratively) To criticize cuttingly.
To cut or attempt to cut, particularly:
(cricket) To swing wildly at the ball.
To strike violently and randomly, particularly:
To move quickly and violently.
To crack a whip with a slashing motion.
(US, Canada) To clear land, (particularly forestry) with violent action such as logging or brushfires or (agriculture, uncommon) through grazing.
(intransitive, fandom slang) To write slash fiction.

quote.citation: 1997 December 17, ASCEM, quoting Ruth Gifford, “Re: An Interesting Question, re Slash vs. Gay Fiction”, in alt.startrek.creative.erotica.moderated‎[1] (Usenet):
quote.text: Having read slash for other fandoms (mainly X-Files and Sentinel), I can say the whole gay issue gets dealt with more often in that slash than it does in Trek slash. That's not to say that all the slashers who slash in a "modern-era" show deal with AIDS, homophobia and other gay issues, but some of them do.

definitions.definition: Used to note the sound or action of a slash.
(Canada, US) Used to connect two or more identities in a list.

quote.citation: 2001, Drake Sather, Ben Stiller, John Hamburg, Zoolander, spoken by Fabio Lanzoni:
quote.text: What this, the Slashie, means is that you consider me the best actor slash model and not the other way around.

quote.citation: 2022 October 2, Tom Phillips, “‘A day of hope’: Lula fans eager to see Bolsonaro defeated”, in The Guardian‎[2]:
quote.text: “It’s been a joke-slash-tragedy,” the restaurant host, 29, said of the president’s tumultuous far-right administration as she cast her vote against him in her country’s most important election in decades.

definitions.definition: (Canada, US) Used to list alternatives.

Alternatives can be marked by the slash/: Alternatives can be marked by the slash-slash-stroke-slash-solidus punctuation mark

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Uncertain. Compare Scots slash (“large splash”), possibly from Old French esclache. Slang use for urination attested from the 1950s.

definitions.definition: (obsolete, rare) A drink of something; a draft.
(UK, slang, vulgar) A piss: an act of urination.
(UK, slang, vulgar, rare) Piss; urine.
(intransitive, UK, slang) To piss, to urinate.

quote.citation: 1973, Martin Amis, The Rachel Papers,, page 189:
quote.text: If you can slash in my bed (I thought) don't tell me you can't suck my cock.

etymologies.etymologyHTML:
Uncertain. Compare British dialectal slashy (“wet and dirty, miry”) and Scots slash (“act of walking forcefully through water or mud”) and slatch (“wet and muddy place, mire”). Perhaps related to Swedish slask (“slush”).

Compare also slash (“clearing in a forest”): in many cases it is difficult to tell whether that sense or this one is meant. (Also compare flash (“a marsh; a pool of water”).)

definitions.definition: (eastern US) A swampy area; a swamp.

quote.citation: 1687, Colonial Virginia Patents 7, page 590, quoted in 1940, George Davis McJimsey, Topographic Terms in Virginia, page 120:
quote.text: On the North side of one of ye Windings of a great Slash or Swamp called ye Roundabout.

quote.citation: 1694, Edmond Andros, Isabella Mackland, colonial Virginia record (granting land to Robert Beverly), quoted in 1988, Beverley Fleet, Virginia Colonial Abstracts, page 318:
quote.text: three acres one Rood and Six pole of Land [...] Extending Northward along the Ditch thirty six poles and two fifths of a pole to a slash called Pitch and Tar Slash or Swamp[,] then along that Slash till it come to the Main Cart road westward [...]

quote.citation: 1694 October 26, colonial Virginia record (regarding Capt. Richard Halle of the County of Essex)m quoted in 1988, Beverley Fleet, Virginia Colonial Abstracts, page 406:
quote.text: 720 acres "lying in the Forrest between Rappahannock and Mattapony river". Adjoins Goldman's land, the line of Robins by and [sic] old Indian path in a slash, the land of Majr Robert Beverley, deceased.

quote.citation: 1714, Colonial Virginia Patents 10, pages 153, 168, quoted in 1940, George Davis McJimsey, Topographic Terms in Virginia, page 121:
quote.text: Thence . . . to two small pines by a Slash or Sunken ground. . . . Thence . . . to two white oaks by a slash in lowground.

quote.citation: 1715, Colonial Virginia Patents 10, 247, quoted in 1940, George Davis McJimsey, Topographic Terms in Virginia, page 121:
quote.text: Beginning at the North side of a Slash incomposeing Long [...]

quote.citation: 1747 September, John Garrott, Virginia deed (of Amelia County, Deed Book 2, page 542) quoted in 1988, Beverley Fleet, Virginia Colonial Abstracts, page 459:
quote.text: 80 acres in Amelia Co., in the fork betw Persimmon Slash and the Gulley[.]

definitions.definition: (eastern US, uncommon) A slash pine, which grows in such (swampy) areas.

quote.citation: 1932, Mr. Yon, statement regarding a waterway from Choctawhatchee Bay to West Bay, Florida, printed in the Hearings of the United States House Committee on Rivers and Harbors (1932), page 8:
quote.text: […]  second growth long-leaf yellow slash. And also we have a short-leaf pine.
Slash pine (Pinus caribaea Morelet) / Slash pine is also known as yellow slash, swamp pine, hill slash, and Cuban pine.]

definitions.definition: (Scotland) A large quantity of watery food such as broth.
(Scotland, intransitive) To work in wet conditions.
(UK) Alternative form of slatch: a deep trough of finely-fractured culm or a circular or elliptical pocket of coal.
